prompt.context: Your client is Foci Pharmaceuticals — a leading rare disease pharmaceutical company — and has seen US sales growth slow down over the past year. Your firm has been hired to determine the cause of this slowdown and recommend ways to reverse the trend.
prompt.question: What is causing Foci Pharmaceuticals' US sales growth to slow down, and what should the client do to reverse this trend?

clarifying_info.q: Does Foci have any direct competitors?
clarifying_info.a: No direct competitors; the client is effectively the market.
100% of revenues come from one drug, Nalparcin, which treats a rare type of muscular dystrophy (MD).

clarifying_info.q: When was Nalparcin launched and is it protected?
clarifying_info.a: Launched in 2017. It is an orphan drug; its FDA exclusivity period lasts through end of 2024, so no generic can be approved until then.

clarifying_info.q: How many patients are eligible for Nalparcin?
clarifying_info.a: Only 30,000 patients in the US are eligible to receive it.

clarifying_info.q: What is the price of treatment?
What type of drug is Nalparcin?
clarifying_info.a: It is a small molecule drug — low molecular weight, able to enter cells easily.

exhibits.title: Foci Pharmaceuticals Revenue Data
exhibits.shows: A chart displaying Foci Pharmaceuticals' annual US revenue figures over recent years, broken down by new versus existing patients, showing slowing revenue growth despite consistent new patient acquisition.
exhibits.data: Revenue trend by year segmented by new vs. existing patient cohorts; growth rate visibly decelerating

exhibits.title: Patient Adherence and Persistence Rates
exhibits.shows: Two bar charts: one showing Patient Adherence Rate grouped by years since starting treatment (1-year / new patients vs. 2+ years / existing patients), and one showing Patient Annual Persistence Rate for the same groups.
exhibits.data: Adherence Rate: 60% for new patients (1 year), 40% for existing patients (2+ years). Persistence Rate: 50% for new patients (1 year), 50% for existing patients (2+ years).

framework: Recognize monopolistic market structure — no competitors, single product, fixed eligible patient pool of 30,000
Break revenue into components: Revenue = # patients × adherence rate × price per day × days per year
Identify the two key revenue levers: market penetration (share of 30,000 eligible patients on treatment) and revenue per patient (driven by adherence and persistence)
Deep-dive patient adherence: are patients taking their daily pill? Each missed pill = ~$1,370 in lost revenue ($500K / 365)
Deep-dive patient persistence: are patients staying on treatment? Patients who drop off stop generating any revenue
Synthesize: consistent new patient acquisition but declining revenue per patient implies adherence and/or persistence are the root cause
Recommend solutions to improve adherence and persistence; evaluate proposed campaign quantitatively

questions.prompt: What are the key components of revenue for Foci, and what might be driving the slowdown?
questions.guidance: Strong answer identifies Revenue = Patients on treatment × Price × Adherence (days taken / days in year). Candidate should note price is fixed at $500K/year and eligible pool is capped at 30,000, so the only growth levers are market penetration (new patients) and revenue per patient (adherence × persistence). Since new patient acquisition is steady, the issue must be revenue per patient — pointing to adherence or persistence declining.

questions.prompt: Given Exhibit 2, what does the adherence and persistence data tell you, and what are the revenue implications?
questions.guidance: Good candidate notes both rates are low: only 60% of new patients adhere daily and only 40% of existing patients adhere; 50% of all patients stop treatment within a year. This means Foci must continuously acquire new patients just to sustain revenue. The low existing-patient adherence (40% vs. 60%) explains why revenue per patient falls as the cohort ages. Each missed pill costs roughly $1,370 ($500,000 / 365 days). Candidate should hypothesize causes and push toward solutions.

math.setup: Revenue per patient per year = $500,000 × adherence rate. Each missed pill costs $500,000 / 365 ≈ $1,370.
steps: New patient annual revenue per patient: $500,000 × 60% = $300,000
Existing patient annual revenue per patient: $500,000 × 40% = $200,000
math.answer: Existing patients generate $100,000 less revenue per year than new patients due to lower adherence.

questions.prompt: The Chief Patient Officer proposes an informational sales and marketing campaign targeting patients and doctors to improve adherence and persistence. The campaign costs $300M. Should Foci implement it? Calculate projected 2021 revenues with and without the campaign. (Campaign effect: adherence +5 percentage points across all cohorts; persistence +10 percentage points across all cohorts. Existing patients at start of 2021: 3,750. New patients acquired in 2021: 4,000, all at start of year. Product margins: 80%.)
questions.guidance: Candidate must organize the math into four buckets: existing patients without/with initiative, new patients without/with initiative. Key technique: since patients drop out continuously, use average patient count during the year = (BoY count + EoY count) / 2. Strong candidate compares incremental profit to campaign cost and notes the campaign does not break even on direct margin but may have longer-term benefits.

math.setup: Average patients during year = (BoY + EoY) / 2 where EoY = BoY × persistence rate. Revenue per cohort = avg patients × adherence rate × $500,000.
steps: WITHOUT INITIATIVE — Existing patients: BoY=3,750; EoY=3,750×50%=1,875; Avg=2,813≈2,800. Revenue=2,800×40%×$500K=$560M
WITHOUT INITIATIVE — New patients: BoY=4,000; EoY=4,000×50%=2,000; Avg=3,000. Revenue=3,000×60%×$500K=$900M
WITH INITIATIVE — Existing patients: BoY=3,750; EoY=3,750×60%=2,250; Avg=3,000. Revenue=3,000×45%×$500K=$675M
WITH INITIATIVE — New patients: BoY=4,000; EoY=4,000×60%=2,400; Avg=3,200. Revenue=3,200×65%×$500K=$1,040M
Campaign cost: $300M — campaign does NOT break even in year one ($204M benefit vs. $300M cost)
math.answer: Without initiative: $1.46B. With initiative: $1.715B. Incremental revenue uplift: $255M (~17%). Incremental profit: $204M. Campaign cost $300M exceeds first-year incremental profit by ~$96M, so it does not break even in 2021.

brainstorming.prompt: What might be causing low patient adherence and low patient persistence for Nalparcin?

categories.name: Patient-related
ideas: Behavioral characteristics — forgetfulness, poor routine, motivation
Demographics — age, literacy, ability to self-administer
Socioeconomic indicators — financial stress, access to pharmacy
Mental health — depression or anxiety related to chronic disease diagnosis

categories.name: Condition-related
ideas: Severity of muscular dystrophy — milder cases may feel less urgency
Perceived efficacy — patients not noticing benefit may discontinue
Disease progression reducing ability to self-administer

categories.name: Drug-related
ideas: Side effects causing patients to skip or stop doses
Pill burden — number of concurrent medications
Complexity of dosing regimen (e.g., timing requirements with food)

categories.name: Health-system related
ideas: Insurance coverage gaps or prior authorization hurdles
Provider characteristics — insufficient counseling or follow-up
Lack of patient support programs or nurse navigators
Specialty pharmacy distribution issues — stockouts or delivery delays

categories.name: Awareness and education
ideas: Patients and caregivers not understanding the importance of daily dosing
Physicians not emphasizing adherence at appointments
Lack of reminder tools or digital adherence aids

recommendation: The root cause of slowing revenue growth is declining patient adherence (especially among existing patients at 40%) and low patient persistence (50% annual dropout rate), not a loss of new patients.

On the proposed campaign: the first-year incremental profit ($204M at 80% margin) does not cover the $300M campaign cost; however, improving adherence and persistence compounds over time and can justify the investment if benefits persist beyond 2021.

Recommendation can go either way — implement the campaign if longer-term compounding benefits and patient health outcomes justify the upfront loss; defer if capital can generate higher returns elsewhere (new indications, pipeline drugs).
risks: Projected adherence and persistence improvements are estimates with significant uncertainty
$300M is a large upfront investment with no guaranteed payback in year one
Root causes of low adherence are unknown, so the campaign content may not address the actual barriers
Exclusivity expires end of 2024, limiting the runway to recoup investment
next_steps: Conduct patient and physician research to identify specific causes of low adherence and persistence before designing campaign content
Model multi-year NPV of the campaign to assess long-term ROI
Explore alternative, lower-cost interventions (digital reminders, nurse navigator programs, patient assistance programs)
Evaluate whether budget could deliver higher returns in pipeline R&D or pursuing additional indications for Nalparcin
Establish KPIs and a rollout plan if campaign is approved
